posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md: I was able to aquire some of the honeycomb surplus and am in the process of making a 10" thick, 4' x 8' table. I'll post photos and results as I have them.

posts.author: John Klayer
posts.content_md: Is your honeycomb material 10" thick or are you going to layer it? How thick will the skins be?

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md: The honeycomb will be 7 layers. I am going to use 11 guage skins. I don't have layers large enough for 4x8 so I will be making 4 piece layers. I am going to use finish cloth fiberglass in between the layers to hold the glue. I plan to use Tap 4 to 1 epoxy as the glue and to prep the steel with 80 grit sanding disks. I then have to rearange the studio to fit it which means I will be giving away my older table if anyone wants to pick it up.

I thought of wood but that would use too much epoxy. I just want to spread the load of the edges of the honeycomb out a little to help the compression strength.

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md:
I have all of the steel and the fiberglass. I just need to pickup some resin. I have a friend who owns a composite manufacturing company and he will be helping with the layup. I should have a new table this week!

I am going to cast in some nuts for attaching an overhead gantry. I am not sure about the design of it however. Is anyone using an overhead reference? Do you have the collimation mirror on the table and a flat mirror overhead or do you just put the collimation mirror overhead?

I am thinking of building the gantry with 1 1/4" pipe filled with sand and sealed with wax. I will have 6 uprights (I think). I am going to make 4' cross sections attached with cheesbourghs. These are cast iron clamps used to attach pipe in high load situations. I use them in theater a lot and they are available from theatrical lighting supply stores for about $20 ea. They also make an adjustable angle version that I am going to use to brace in some diagonals for extra stiffness.

I am haveing a hard time figuring out what height I should make the gantry. Any thoughts?

posts.author: BobH
posts.content_md: I've mounted a 17.5" collimating mirror 4' off the table, pointing down. Just don't forget to make it earthquake safe! A safety chain saved mine, in Boulder Creek during the Loma Prieta quake. I was in Los Angeles, installing Images in Time & Space, and returned to see the mirror, tilted forward and hanging from the chain over table that did a little dance while I was away.

posts.author: MichaelH
posts.content_md:
fwiw my gantry is 3' high (it's the highest I could go and still get the laser on top and under the canopy) and I used 1" electrical conduit for the piping filled with sand and sealed with silicone. I started out hanging my collimating mirror but at the moment I'm happier just putting the laser on the gantry and using the new collimator mount I made several weeks ago.

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md: Well, then why use a sandwich structure at all? I think the key is to have the entire table move as one solid, rigid structure in the presence of any movement at all. Thus if a vibration was propogating from ground from the East the East leg would transfer the vibration first to the table. If the table was not rigid this would cause a wave(s) to travel down the table from the East leg to the West leg, the table itself would be the wave. If the table is rigid the entire table would move but not as a wave but a stiff board riding that wave. All components on the table would remain fixed relative to one another. Weight (mass) causes a dampening of that wave. More mass, more wave energy is needed to move that mass a specific distance.

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md:
> **VR:** Remember that the honey comb only needs to take shear loads.So, do we really need to glue the pieces together at all?

I think so.It is the same question as "Do we need to glue the edge of the cans together in a can table?" If you imagine the top plate moving in an oposite direction from the bottom plate (shear) then having cans glued together on their sides will make them less likely to tip over. Honey comb is not so extreme of an example but I think some glue would be in order. Microbaloons are cheap and easy to work with.
